Based on the data you provided, the short answer is: **It is highly unlikely that you would be able to see the Moon right now.**

Here is the breakdown of why you can probably relax:

### 1. The "Daylight Washout" Effect
Even though the Moon is technically above the horizon (at an altitude of about 16 degrees), the Sun is much higher in the sky (at 56 degrees). Because the Sun is so high and the sky is "bright daylight," the atmosphere is flooded with scattered sunlight. This creates a massive amount of "background noise" in the sky. 

For a Moon that is only **25% illuminated** (a thin crescent), there isn't enough surface area reflecting light to compete with the brightness of the daytime sky.

### 2. The Geometry (The "Sun Angle")
The Moon is only 60 degrees away from the Sun. In astronomy, when the Moon is that close to the Sun in the sky during the day, it is almost always lost in the glare. To see a crescent moon during the day, it usually needs to be much lower toward the horizon (where the atmosphere can sometimes provide a bit of contrast) or the Sun needs to be much lower.

### 3. Your Visual Perspective
Since you have "normal unaided eyesight," your pupils will be constricted due to the bright daylight. This significantly reduces your ability to see faint objects. To see a 25% illuminated moon in broad daylight, you would likely need a pair of high-powered binoculars or a telescope to "isolate" it from the surrounding glare.

### Summary
While your app correctly identifies that the Moon is physically "up" in the sky, it is effectively "hidden" by the sheer brilliance of the day. Unless you are looking directly toward the Sun (which you shouldn't do!) or have specialized equipment, **the Moon will be invisible to your eyes.**

You can breathe a sigh of relief—it's not going to pop out at you!
